A general statement of policy, on the other hand, does not 
estabhsh a ‘^binding norm.” It is not finally determinative of the 
issues or rights to which it is addressed. The agency cannot apply 
or rely upon a general statement of pohcy as law because a general 
statement of pohcy only announces what the agency seeks to 
estabhsh as pohcy. A pohcy statement announces the agency’s 
tentative intentions for the future. When the agency apphes the 
pohcy in a particular situation, it must be prepared to support the 
pohcy just as if the pohcy statement had never been issued. An 
agency cannot escape its responsibihty to present evidence and 
reasoning supporting its substantive rules by announcing binding 
precedent in the form of a general statement of pohcy.
In Community Nutrition Institute v. Young, 818 F.2d 943, 948 (D.C. 
Cir. 1987), the court imphedly qualified Pacific Gas, The case concerned 
the FDA, which had adopted “action levels” for ubiquitous contaminants, 
such as lead and mercury, to guide its field inspectors in assessing whether 
specific foods should be seized and destroyed for non-comphance with the 
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The action levels, in FDA’s words, were to 
“to define the level of contamination at which food will be deemed to be 
adulterated” by FDA itself, for purposes of initiating enforcement 
proceedings that, if they ran their full course, would be concluded through 
agency-as-plaintiff suits for enforcement in federal court. Food-safety 
activists who feared that certain action levels were too low sued FDA, 
contending that the action levels were legislative rules and therefore 
invalid, because they had been adopted without notice and comment. FDA 
responded that its action levels were pohcy statements, conceding (along 
the fines of Pacific Gas) that it would have to establish the validity of the 
action levels themselves, and not merely establish that they had been 
violated, in subsequent enforcement proceedings. The D.C. Circuit found 
FDA’s concession insufficient to rescue the action levels from invalidation 
as legislative rules:
We are not unmindful that in a suit to enjoin shipment of allegedly 
contaminated corn, it appears that FDA would be obliged to prove 
that the corn is “adulterated,” within the meaning of the FDC Act, 
rather than merely prove non-compliance with the action level. 
* * * The action level thus does not bind food producers in the 
sense that producers are automatically subject to enforcement 
proceedings for violating the action level. This factor, accordingly, 
points in favor of the agency’s characterization. But the fact that 
action levels do not completely bind food producers as would a 
more classic legislative rule (where the only issue before the court 
would be if the agency rule were in fact violated) is not 
determinative of the issue. For here, we are convinced that FDA
